catalog_quote: [p.152, sec. 11 TONE TYPOLOGY] Tone is a prominent feature of all Lakes Plain languages and therefore was most likely a feature of some of the protolanguages as well. This fact further distances Lakes Plain languages from the Trans New Guinea Phylum. All the modem languages have at least high and low tone. Duvle and Sikaritai have only these tones with Martin (1991) analysing the Sikaritai system as pitch-accent. [p.160, Appendix 3] Although tonal contrast is found in virtually all of the the Lakes Plain languages, it will not be shown in the word list transcriptions. Additionally, stress is not marked because only a few original word lists marked it and it has not been found to be contrastive in any of the Lakes Plain languages to date. ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level generalisation only: all Lakes Plain languages (Awera included by membership) are tonal with at least H and L; stress has not been found contrastive in any Lakes Plain language. No statement of where stress falls, and nothing Awera-specific on prosody; for Awera the author's only data are a 1987 survey wordlist (p.141 'the only data that do exist are word lists').
new_statements.exceptions: none; Sikaritai analysed as pitch-accent (Martin 1991) is the only per-language prosodic qualification, not relevant to Awera
new_statements.domain_note: Comparative overview based on survey word lists; remarks concern transcription conventions for isolated citation forms, not an analysis of Awera word prosody.
new_statements.identity_note: Single-village language: Clouse 1997 gives the wordlist village as 'Awera'; the SIL archive record of the same Jones Feb-1987 list gives 'Wapoga Village, Waropen Regency' (Awera village lies in Wapoga District; the village is majority Ansus-speaking per Wikipedia/Clouse). Same variety, glottocode awer1241; no dialects reported.
